lesson.title: Red, Green, Refactor: Writing Tests Before You Write Code
lesson.summary: Test-driven development is a workflow where you write a failing test before the code that satisfies it, then write just enough code to pass, then refactor with the test as a safety net.
lesson.body:
Most beginning programmers write code first and think about testing it later, if at all. Test-driven development flips that order: you write a test that describes the behavior you want, watch it fail, and only then write the code that makes it pass. It sounds backwards until you try it, and then it becomes hard to go back.

The workflow has three repeating steps, often called red, green, refactor. First, red: you write a small test for a piece of behavior that does not exist yet, and you run it to confirm it fails, which matters more than it sounds, because a test that passes by accident, perhaps because of a typo in the function name, tells you nothing. Second, green: you write the smallest, simplest amount of code that makes that test pass, resisting the urge to build in extra features you have not written a test for yet. Third, refactor: with a passing test as your safety net, you clean up the code, improve names, remove duplication, or simplify logic, then rerun the test to confirm it still passes. Then you repeat the cycle for the next piece of behavior.

This builds directly on unit testing, the practice of writing small, focused tests that each check one behavior of one piece of code. TDD does not introduce a new kind of test; it changes when you write the tests you already know how to write, moving them before the implementation instead of after. The payoff is that the test forces you to decide, in concrete terms, what the function should do before you get lost in how to do it. It also means you never end up with untested code, because the tests were the first thing you wrote.

Consider building a function called clamp(value, low, high) that restricts a number to a range. You start red: you write test_clamp_within_range that asserts clamp(5, 0, 10) equals 5, and run it. It fails immediately, since clamp does not exist yet. Green: you write the smallest thing that passes, def clamp(value, low, high): return value. The test passes, but the function is obviously incomplete, which is fine, because you have not written a test that would catch that yet. Next test, red again: test_clamp_below_range asserts clamp(-5, 0, 10) equals 0. It fails, since the current function just returns value unchanged. Green: you add a check, if value < low: return low, else return value. That test passes. One more cycle: test_clamp_above_range asserts clamp(15, 0, 10) equals 10, which fails until you add the matching check for the upper bound. Now, refactor: with all three tests passing, you notice the three branch version can be written more simply as return max(low, min(value, high)). You make the change, rerun all three tests, and they still pass, so you know the simplification did not change the behavior.

That last step is the real value of TDD. Refactoring code without tests is a leap of faith; refactoring code with tests is a checked move. The tests you wrote first become a permanent regression suite: if someone changes clamp() next year and breaks the upper bound behavior, the test fails immediately, at the moment of the change, instead of showing up as a mysterious bug three features later.
